# The Commerce deck

**What it rewards:** Wealth from connection. Trade routes, trading posts, partnerships, resource wealth and deliberate spending. The deck is weak at production; it buys what other empires build and turns gold into production. **Directions inside it:** mining districts and mineral exports; luxury stockpiles and monopolies; domestic provisioning; overseas posts and exploration; reserves versus purchased capability.

*Initially generated by `scripts/deckDocs.mjs`; now a hand-edited design spec (deck-list pass, 2026-10-06). **Built** means the effect exists in the game, **revised** means this sheet changes a live effect, **new** means a card proposed in the deck-list pass of 2026-10-06 (its last column says whether existing effects can express it or what it needs), and **deferred** means the proposed effect is not implemented. Government tiers here are proposed availability, not confirmation of runtime unlocks. The generator runs only on request and overwrites these edits.*

> Your inline revisions are folded into the tables. Names for previously unnamed proposals are provisional; unspecified rarities and new cards’ tiers/rarities are editorial proposals. Existing placements, stated rarities and numerical changes are retained.

**Mining line:** Tier 0 exchanges mine/quarry production for gold. Tier I adds strategic-resource yields and mineral exports; Tier II rewards mine clusters and extra luxury copies; Tier III lets customs houses and manufactories join the mining economy. Private Patronage remains in Tier I, and Merchant Works remains the Tier IV project payoff. Tile yield bonuses require the tile to be worked; mine adjacency and origin-city mine counts do not require every counted mine to be worked.

What makes it different from every other card in the game is that it changes what a player may **see** rather than what a player gets — the first of its kind — and a seat that can see a rival's queue is a seat the server will one day have to be careful what it sends. (2) The ledger is read two ways, as a *narrowing* on the moment it happened and as a *count* of what it holds, and this card wants the count — the shape exists (the faith one is counted exactly that way) but there is no member for roads. ## Tier II

| Card | Rarity | Status | The card | What the game does, or why not |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Numidian Cavalry *(charter)*** | uncommon | deferred | Once drafted, unlock Numidian Cavalry, a Horseman replacement. No chair required. Gains +1 combat strength per distinct luxury you control; luxuries obtained only through the Silk Road contribute +0.5 instead. Normal technology requirements apply. | Held whole, and the hole is a roster row rather than a shape. A charter can already open a building or a technology but not a unit, and the horse it would open has not been drawn. The strength that grows with the goods you hold is ordinary law; the half-strength for a borrowed good is not, because nothing asks whether one particular luxury arrived on loan. |
| **Strategic Exports** | uncommon | built | Trade routes gain +1 science per improved strategic resource deposit in their origin city. Your strategic resource deposits provide twice their normal quantity. | +1 science on every trade route you send, once for every improved strategic seam inside the borders of the town it left · your strategic seams supply twice as many copies. **The second sentence touches no ground at all**, which is the user's ruling (2026-09-19): the seams on the map are what they always were, and what doubles is the total your realm holds. Three things make that exact. It is taken of the copies your **own** opened seams supply, so a copy another empire lent you is not doubled and a copy you lent away comes off the doubled figure rather than being doubled with it. It reaches strategic rows only, asked of the table's own word for a kind. And it is applied **outside** the walk that is remembered from turn to turn: that walk is kept on a clock the taking-up of a card does not move, so a law read inside it would leave every count stale for the rest of the turn — and a stale copy count is a unit a seat can or cannot build, which is how a played game starts disagreeing with a replay of its own log. Royal Assays and The Warehouses are **not** opened by this: they want a seam's own quantity and a doubling aimed at one named good, which are different questions from an empire-wide share of a total. |
| **Purchased Prosperity** | uncommon | built | You may purchase tiles with gold while your authority is negative. If you have purchased a tile in the last 5 turns, all your cities gain +1 happiness. | you may still buy hexes while your authority is overdrawn · buying a hex grants +1 happiness in every city for the next five turns, however often it happens. **C2's note had the two halves the wrong way round.** The first sentence was the easy one: the freeze that stops an overdrawn realm buying ground is a single refusal, and this is one more clause on it, exactly as the wonder counter and the capital's purchase limit are lifted. The second was the hard one: a moment could hang a contentment on the realm, but it *stacked* — a second hex inside the window paid a second point, where the card promises one standing fact with a fresh end date. A timed grant may now say it renews, which rewrites its own expiry instead of adding a second entry. This row had never been entered in the data at all; C4 wrote it. |
| **Mining Districts** | uncommon | built | Worked mines gain +1 gold and +1 science for every two adjacent mines. | +1 gold, +1 science on every hex with a Mine, once for every two hexes with a Mine beside it. The divisor is the same field a counted line already uses, read in one more place. The neighbours need not be worked or yours; the mine being paid must be worked, as every line that lands on a hex must. Odd numbers round down. This is the first live row to use the per-neighbour reading at all. |
| **Royal Assays** | uncommon | built | Each improved luxury resource deposit with a mine provides one additional copy of that luxury. | each of your luxury deposits with a mine supplies one more copy. It went through the same door Strategic Exports opened, and the decomposition C7 built is what made it safe: the map walk is remembered on a clock a card does not move, so the walk now reports two ground facts — the copies your deposits supply, and how many of those deposits carry a mine — and the law is applied on the way out. Everything C7 established holds unchanged. No tile is written; the figure is your realm's total. It reaches the term your **own** deposits supply, so a copy lent to you is untouched and a copy you lent away comes off the raised figure. And it is luxuries only, asked of the table's own word for a kind. What is different is the arithmetic: a flat step per deposit rather than a share of a total, because "each deposit provides one additional copy" is a count and half again on three seams is not one more from each. This row had never been entered in the data at all; C8 wrote it. |
| **Civic Markets** | common | built | Markets provide +2 science and +2 food. | +2 food, +2 science in every city with a Market |
| **Luxury Caravans** | common | built | Trade routes gain +1 gold for every luxury resource tile in their origin city. | +1 gold on every trade route you send, once for every hex carrying a luxury resource inside the borders of the town it left. The card says *tile*, so this counts ground and not kinds: two vineyards in one town are two, and neither has to be improved or worked. The same count as Ore Caravans, asked a different question about the hex. |
| **Maritime Authority** | common | built | Gain +3 authority. Naval units gain +5 combat strength against cities. | +3 authority capacity · +5 combat strength for ships against cities |
| **Professional Retainers** | common | built | All units gain +3 combat strength and cost +1 gold in maintenance. | +3 combat strength · all units cost 1 more gold in maintenance |
| **The Home Market** | common | built | Cities receiving at least two of your domestic routes gain +20% food, +20% production and +2 happiness, once per city. | +20% food, +20% production and +2 happiness in every city that two or more trade routes between your own cities end at. The old note was right about the gap and C5 closed it: the question a town could be asked was a yes and not a tally, and it is a tally now — how many trade routes meet this town, narrowed by which way they run and by whose town is at the far end. One walk answers it, so the yes-or-no three live cards already ask and the counts these three new ones ask cannot drift apart. The happiness is paid once per city however many carts arrive, which is the card's "once per city". The same change opened The League of Cities and The Chartered Metropolis. |
| **The Caravanserai Network** | common | built | Each city receiving a domestic trade route grants +1 happiness (once per city); +1 production and +1 gold on domestic trade routes. | +1 happiness in every city one of your own trade routes ends at · +1 production, +1 gold on every trade route between two of your own cities |
| **The Foreign Factor** | common | built | Each foreign city holding your established commercial post grants you +3 gold and its host city +1 gold per turn while you are at peace and the host is not blockaded. | +3 gold a turn for every foreign city holding your trading post · +1 gold a turn in each of those cities, paid to whoever owns it. Both halves count the same houses, so the coin you take and the coin your host takes can never drift apart. The two provisos are not this card's clauses at all — they are the rule every post follows, written once where a post is read: a post pays nobody while its holder and the host are at war, or while the host city is blockaded. Nothing is lost while either holds; the house is still there when the war ends. |
| **The Capital Arsenal** | uncommon | built | There is no limit on the number of units that can be purchased per turn in your capital. | Your capital may buy as many units in a turn as it can pay for. One named rule, read beside the one place the one-a-turn stamp is compared against. The stamp is still written, so a seat that loses the card is back under the limit the same turn; every other refusal at the counter still stands, including needing somewhere to put the unit. The capital is named in the rule itself because a named rule carries no scope. |
| **The Purple Works *(charter)*** | rare | deferred | Once drafted, unlock the Purple Works for construction. No chair required. This national building supplies one manufactured luxury copy; its payload is specified below. | Held whole. The works it would open has not been drawn up yet, and neither has the good it would make. |
| **The Chartered Arsenal** | uncommon | built | Military units purchased with gold gain +4 strength permanently on creation. | newly created military units bought with gold gain +4 combat strength |
| **The Harbour Chain** | uncommon | built | Gain +1 route capacity per two Harbours you own, at most +4. Sea routes gain +3 range and +1 gold for every 4 hexes travelled. | +1 trade route per two Harbours, at most four · sea trade routes reach three turns further · +1 gold on a sea trade route for every four hexes between its two towns. The first sentence was written for this card by name in D2b and was only waiting. The other two needed one word each. **A card may say "sea" now:** a trade route's pay may be narrowed by the medium it takes, which is a fact about the route rather than about either of its towns — the same kind of narrowing as which side of a border it crosses, read in the same place and worded in the same breath. And how far a caravan may be sent by sea joined the short list of figures a law may move, which is the one-line move a route's term already was. The share is taken of the rules table's own reach and the trading posts' turns are added **after** it, so the card adds exactly the three turns it prints however many posts the pair holds — taking it of the sum would have quietly paid more to a well-established pair. |
| **The League of Cities** | rare | built | Cities with one of your paying outgoing routes gain +15% production and cost one less authority, minimum one. Cities without one lose 10% gold. | +15% production and one less authority in every city a trade route sets out from · -10% gold in every city none sets out from. **"Paying" means active** (the user's ruling, 2026-09-19): a route that has lapsed, been cancelled or been plundered is not counted, and there is no second test behind the word. Three things the old note called missing are all there now. Routes *leaving* a town are the same tally as routes arriving, asked from the other end. The mirror is the tally's own ceiling rather than a second named question — "at most none" — so the reward and its mirror name the same direction and the same kind of route, which two separate members could have drifted apart on. And what one town costs to hold is a figure a law moves; the floor works both ways, so the discount never takes a town below one and never starts charging a town that was already free. |
| **The Charter Fleet** | uncommon | built | Naval combat units cost 20% less gold to purchase. Naval combat units you purchase with gold gain +1 movement permanently. | ships cost −20% to buy · newly created ships bought with gold gain +1 movement. The revision from sight to movement is what opened it: a piece has always been able to be born with a longer march, and a card had no way to say so until now. |
| **The Exchange** | uncommon | deferred | Each different foreign empire your routes currently serve grants +5% science and culture empire-wide. Foreign routes to your cities grant +2 science and +2 culture to both you and the sender. | **The sheet's text is ratified and the data row was brought into line with it** (C8). C7 was right that the first sentence is writable today — a counted line pays a share per helping perfectly well, a live great-person row already gives a share of science and culture for every foreign realm your trade routes reach off the very same count, and two Orders do the same off other counts. That half is a pair of ordinary rows whenever this is taken up. **The second sentence is still the blocker, and the ratified wording makes it a harder one than the capital version was.** A card is only ever consulted about a trade route from the end that *sent* the cart — the law that rides a road is the sender's law, asked of the sender's empire — and the empire holding this card is the end the cart *arrives* at. So this card is never asked about the road at all, which is a new kind of gap: not a missing payee but a missing reading. On top of that, "the sender" is an empire that is neither the card holder nor the town a caravan reached, so it is a third kind of payee besides the two that exist. Both would have to be built. Held whole rather than half-lit, per the deck's house rule. |
| **Foreign Procurement** | uncommon | built | Ignore strategic resource requirements when purchasing units. All units cost 20% more. | A unit you buy needs none of the strategic resources it would need to be built · all units cost 20% more to buy. The waiver is for the counter alone — the queue still refuses a knight with no horses — and it lifts both refusals, "you have none" and "every copy is spoken for". "All units cost 20% more" is read as the purchase price and not production, because both of the card's sentences are about the till. A piece bought this way is ordinary afterwards and still takes a copy, so an empire that buys past its iron finds the iron spoken for. The balance question the old note raised is still open. |
| **The Endowment** | common | built | Purchased buildings provide +2 science. | +2 science in every city per purchased building there. C4's measurement was exact and the missing piece was the only one: a town now records **which bank paid for each of its roofs**, beside the turn they went up, written by the one seam that puts stones in a town and by nothing else (schema 123). It replaces nothing — the ledger of firsts still marks a town's first purchase, and still cannot say which roof it was — because the two answer different questions. Either bank counts: a library bought with faith is as bought as one bought with gold, which is what the word "purchased" says. A roof completed in the yard, granted by a card, raised as a founding Monument or laid as a relic records nothing, and absence is the shape every town saved before the field already had. A captured town brings the record with it, so a conqueror is paid for the roofs its last owner bought — pay follows the stones, as everywhere else. **The sheet's text is the one built**; the data row had drifted to a much larger sentence about a quarter of every native yield, and that is gone. |
| **The Brokers' Redraw** | rare | built | You may reroll a draft with gold instead of faith. All other purchasing is 10% more expensive. | **Ruled: gold at a premium.** you may pay gold for a fresh hand, at a higher price than faith would ask · everything you buy costs 10% more. The redraw command carries a bank now, the way a purchase always has; the gold price is the faith ladder's own figure multiplied, so faith stays the cheaper route and the card is a convenience rather than a replacement. The multiple is a row in the statecraft sheet, not a number in the code. The ladder itself is untouched — either bank climbs the same rungs and raises the same count — and a hand whose first asking is free stays free in both. **Known gap:** nothing on screen offers the gold button yet; the rule and its price are live in the simulation, and the rail that names a bank is a UI pass. |
| **The Scholars' Roads** | rare | built | Lose 4 route capacity. Your routes gain +2 science and +2 culture, and gain +50% science and culture. | -4 trade routes · +2 science, +2 culture on every trade route you send · +50% science and culture on every trade route you send |

Cities with a customs house gain +15% gold toward purchasing. | +3 gold on every hex with a Customs House · +1 renown a turn for every Customs House inside your borders · everything costs 15% less to buy in a town whose borders hold one. The coin wants a citizen standing on the works, as every hex line does; the renown and the discount do not. "+15% gold toward purchasing" is read as a discount of that size. |

Merchant missionaries, for Commerce and Devotion. |

## Tier III

| Card | Rarity | Status | The card | What the game does, or why not |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **The Masters' Guild** | rare | deferred | Gain +5 renown. Customs houses and manufactories receive all mine bonuses and count as mines. | Held whole, and this one is a genuine hole rather than a missing field. The renown is one line. "Counts as a mine" asks the board to answer a question about one work with another work's name — every clause that asks what stands on a hex would have to consult the law first, which is a new kind of thing for the ground to do, not a new card shape. |
| **Caravanserai Cities** | uncommon | built | Caravanserais can be built in every city. Cities with a Caravanserai gain +20% gold. | you may build a Caravanserai in every city · +20% gold in every city holding one. **Ruled: a caravanserai stays an empire building** (the user, 2026-09-19: *"we need two different flags, can be built once and is empire building"*). So the mark that limited the house and the mark that classed it are two marks now, and every building that carried the old one carries both — nothing about any existing row moved. The card lifts the **limit** and leaves the **class** exactly where it was, which is the whole of why it is coherent: a realm may raise a yard in every town, and every one of them is still priced against how many towns it will serve, still admitted wherever a card asks for a town holding one of the realm's great houses, still counted as one of them, and still passed over by a discount written for the ordinary shelves. The card buys many of an expensive thing rather than turning it into a cheap one. One thing had to be made safe alongside it: the walk that gathers what a realm's great houses do used to read each town's shelf in turn, which was harmless while a realm could hold only one of each, so it now reads each row **once** however many copies stand — otherwise the yard's own gift to every caravan leaving that town would have been paid once per yard. This row had never been entered in the data at all; C4 entered it deferred and C7 lit it. |
| **Entrenched Interests** | uncommon | built | Your units gain +3 combat strength in cities holding your trading post, including foreign cities. Going to war does not remove these posts. | +3 combat strength for any unit of yours standing in a city that holds your trading post. Who owns the city is deliberately not asked, which is the card's "including foreign cities". The second sentence is not a clause anywhere — it is what a post *is*: a post is established by trading and is then permanent, and war suspends only the income. So this is the one card that reads the footprint rather than the income, and it goes on paying against the very empire you built the house with. This row was on the sheet and had never been entered in the data; it was written here. |
| **A Court of Merchants** | rare | built | Gain +50% renown, but great-person offers contain only Great Merchants. | **Ruled: fall back to the normal draw.** +50% renown a turn · every great-person offer shows only great merchants, until there are none left to call. The share is taken of the whole recurring trickle and never of a triumph's lump. The narrowing is a strong nudge and not a lock: when every great merchant in the world has been called, the draft goes back to the whole roster, so the standing rule that a spent roster banks rather than blocks survives. A draft somebody bought narrowed to another family — the Academy's scholars — is dealt as what it was bought as. This row had never been entered in the data at all; C3 wrote it. |
| **The Warehouses** | uncommon | deferred | For each resource of which you control at least 4 copies, double its resource effect and gain +8 culture and +10 gold. | **The data row was brought into line with the sheet** (C8; it had drifted to a sentence about four improved deposits paying gold, culture and contentment). The counting half is much closer than when C4 wrote its note: copies are real and countable at empire scale, and asking which goods a realm holds four or more of is that same reading with a threshold. What is still missing there is the threshold itself — the one the game asks about duplicates is fixed at two, in the meter rather than on a card, so a card cannot name its own figure. **The doubling is the real blocker and it has not moved.** "Double *its* resource effect" aims a doubling at one named good, and every dial in the vocabulary turns a whole class at once — the flat happiness every luxury pays, what a duplicate copy is worth, what a realm's strategic deposits supply. A dial that reached one row would be a new kind of amplifier and a design decision. Held whole. |
| **The Money Lenders** | rare | built | Earn interest equal to 2% of your treasury each turn, with no cap. | +1 gold per 50 gold in the treasury — a coin for every fiftieth, which is the two per hundred the card quotes, floored once. The old ceiling and the purchasing surcharge are both gone with the revision. |
| **The Dye Vats *(charter)*** | uncommon | deferred | Once drafted, unlock the Dye Vats for construction. No chair required. This purchased building turns its city's worked luxuries toward culture and faith; its payload is specified below. | Held whole. The vats they would open have not been drawn up yet, so the charter has nothing to grant. |
| **The Paid Army** | uncommon | built | Military-unit upkeep falls by 1 gold, minimum zero. Military units cost 25% less gold to purchase. | military units cost 1 less gold in maintenance · military units cost −25% to buy |
| **The Chartered Metropolis** | rare | built | Cities with at least three of your paying outgoing routes gain +25% food, production and culture, but each costs +4 authority while qualified. | +25% food, +25% production and +25% culture in every city three or more trade routes set out from · +4 authority for each such city. All three of the old note's gaps closed together in C5. **"Paying" means active** (the user's ruling, 2026-09-19) — a lapsed, cancelled or plundered route is not counted, and nothing else is tested. "While qualified" falls out of the shape rather than needing a clause: the surcharge is a scoped repricing asked fresh every turn, so a city that drops to two routes stops paying it that turn. |
| **The Admiralty of Trade** | rare | built | Your sea routes may connect two cities holding your established commercial posts regardless of range. A legal sea path, access, peace and route capacity are still required. | a sea trade route between two towns that both hold your trading post may be sent any distance. One named rule read at the one place the gate prices a route's reach, beside the clause it lifts — the shape three other live cards in this deck use for a refusal. It is narrow on purpose. The route must run **by sea**; both towns must hold a post of yours that is actually **paying**, so a war or a blockade suspends the privilege exactly as it suspends a post's income (the design says "card range privileges" in those words, so this is the rule every post follows rather than a clause of this card's); and one post is not two. The card's second sentence is then true by construction rather than by a second reading: every other clause of the gate still runs, so a sea lane no caravan could sail, a partner you have not met, a war, a full slot table and a trade route already running that way are all still refused. |
| **The Merchant Commonwealth** | uncommon | built | Each owned city with your established commercial post receiving a domestic route gains +2 happiness and costs one less authority, minimum one. | +2 happiness and one less authority in every one of your cities that both holds your trading post and has one of your own trade routes ending in it. **C1's note was already half out of date when it was written**: what one town costs to hold became a figure a law may move in D2b, and The League of Cities has been using it since C5 — so the post was the only thing still missing. The two questions are asked of the same town every turn, so a trade route that lapses takes the contentment and the discount with it while the house stays. The floor works both ways: never below one authority, and never a charge on a town that was already free. |
| **The Gilded Scaffold** | rare | built | You may purchase world wonders. All your cities lose 15% production. | **Ruled: build it as written.** you may buy world wonders with gold · -15% production in every city. The lift is a second clause on the one `if` that refuses a wonder at the counter, beside the faith lift the Valley of Kings already had — not a second way to buy one — so every gate below it is asked unchanged: a wonder another empire has claimed, one whose technology is not in, and one whose site the ground does not hold are all still refused. The price is the row's full cost in hammers at the ordinary gold rate. What the refusal protected is now paid for by the card's other half rather than by the rule. |
| **The Toll Roads** | uncommon | new | Each foreign trade route whose path crosses your territory pays you +2 gold a turn, and +1 culture if the path runs along one of your roads. | New. Needs: a trade route's path as a reading (the same need as The Waystations), and a payee who neither sent the trade route nor hosts it. Tolls are a spec theme no other card covers. |
| **The Art Market** | uncommon | new | Landmarks worked by a city with a Market gain +2 gold. Trade routes leaving a city whose borders hold a landmark gain +2 culture. | New. Fits existing effects: a tile line narrowed by a building in the town, and a route line narrowed by a work inside the origin's borders (the same question as The Customs Service). Landmarks on trade routes, for Commerce and Magisterial. |
| **The Company Army *(charter)*** | uncommon | new | Once drafted, unlock Company Infantry, a military unit that can only be bought with gold and never trained. No chair required. Normal technology requirements apply. | New. Needs: a charter that opens a unit (Numidian Cavalry's blocker) and the unit's row. A unit sold only for gold already works: a unit row that names its own bank sells only there. Charters for gold-bought units, for Commerce and Dominion. |
| **A Guild Commission *(commission)*** | uncommon | new | Commission. Goal: buy five buildings with gold while seated. Reward: a free great-person draft, the same offer Merchant Princes sells for gold. The card then leaves its chair. | New. Needs: commissions. The reward is an offer the game already prices. For Commerce and Magisterial. |
| **The Monopoly** | rare | new | For each luxury of which you hold at least three copies and no other empire holds any, gain +5 gold and +3 culture, and every city gains +1 happiness. | New. Needs: a reading of whether any other empire holds a given luxury. Counts of your own copies exist; nothing asks about other empires' copies of one good. Monopolies are a spec theme no other card covers. |
| **The Condottieri** | rare | new | You may hire any military unit you can build for half its gold price. A hired unit costs no upkeep, serves for 15 turns and then leaves. | New. Needs: hired units with an end date. A timed effect on a unit already compares against an absolute turn, but no unit removes itself when a date passes. Mercenary contracts, for Commerce and Dominion. **Overlap:** the same idea is on Dominion's sheet as "Mercenary Contracts"; a candidate for one shared card. |

| Card | Rarity | Status | The card | What the game does, or why not |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Foreign-route empire gold and conversion outputs are excluded from the production basis. | 25% of the gold in every city building a wonder or an empire building is gained again as production · -20% gold in those same cities. The condition was the whole of the gap and it is closed: the queue could be asked what *kind* of row stands at the front and not whether that row is one of the realm's single great houses, which is the marker two other shapes already read. The Opus is an empire building by the data's own declaration, so the card's three classes are two clauses. The exclusions the card names fall out on their own — a conversion reads the town's flat coin before any conversion spoke, and coin a foreign road brings home is an empire figure and never a town's. Only the front of the queue counts. |

## Cards Commerce shares with another deck

A Commerce seat may draw every one of these, and so may a seat holding the deck named beside it — a shared card is spent out of two shelves, so a change here is felt in two decks. Listed in tier order.

| Card | Rarity | Also in | Status | The card | What the game does, or why not | Government tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Market Gardens** | common | Expansionist | built | Farms beside a road gain +1 gold. Domestic routes grant an additional +1 food to their destination. | +1 gold on every hex with a Farm beside a road · +1 food on every trade route between two of your own cities | 0 |
| **Travelling Players** | uncommon | Magisterial | revised | Foreign routes from a city with a Monument gain +1 culture; additional +2 culture for every unique deck type slotted in your government. | **Revised on this sheet.** Was: foreign routes from a city with a Monument gain +2 culture. Live today: +2 culture on every trade route sent from every city with a Monument and that ends in another empire’s city | 2
| **The Escorted Roads** | uncommon | Dominion | built | Routes whose origin has a garrison gain +3 gold. Naval units gain +2 strength while adjacent to one of your traders. | +3 gold on every trade route sent from every city with a unit standing in it · +2 combat strength for ships while standing beside trader units | I |
| **Pilgrim Markets** | uncommon | Devotion | built | Routes gain +2 gold and +2 faith if either endpoint contains a Holy Site. This pays once per route even when both endpoints qualify. | +2 gold and +2 faith on every trade route with either end in a city holding a Holy Site. Both gaps closed, and the first was smaller than it looked. **Faith was missing from a caravan by omission, not by design** — the field's own note said it stayed out "because nothing pays it", which was an absence for want of a card rather than a rule. It was also already a live gap: Mansa Musa's The Hajj has printed "+2 faith" on a road since it was written, and the fold had no field to put the figure in, so the words promised it and the ledger paid none. The voice joined the line the same way science and culture did, is summed by the one fold and is staged and banked by the same code as the five beside it — so the caravan, the trade panel, the Ledger and the town's basket all read the one figure. The second gap is a new narrowing: a route line may now be admitted when **one** of its two towns answers, where the two existing clauses ask about the origin and the destination and are joined by *and*. It is a boolean, so a road with a shrine at both ends is one admitted road and pays once — the card's second sentence, true by construction rather than by a clause. A preview with no far end chosen is promised nothing, which is what the crossing and the destination clauses already do. The site is the prophet's work on the ground and nobody has to be standing on it. **Lives in the shared file, so lighting it changes what Devotion deals too.** It also unblocks two Devotion rows that C6 found waiting on exactly "a trade route carries no faith" — The Alms Roads and The Pilgrim Road — which are outside this batch's fence and untouched. | I |
| **Merchant Scholars** | uncommon | Scientific | revised | Foreign routes gain +2 science for every great work improvement in the origin city. | **Revised on this sheet.** Was: foreign routes from a city with a Library gain +3 science. Live today: +3 science on every trade route sent from every city with a Library and that ends in another empire’s city | I
| **The Grain Exchange** | uncommon | Expansionist | built | Domestic routes from a city with a Granary give +3 food to their destination. Cities receiving one gain +1 happiness. | +3 food on every trade route between two of your own cities sent from a town with a Granary · +1 happiness in every town one of those particular trade routes ends at. The first sentence was an ordinary route line all along. The second needed one field: C5's tally could say how many trade routes meet a town, by direction and by whose town sits at the far end, but never **what the far end holds** — so that is a narrowing on the same tally now, and it is the same walk, which is what keeps the grain and the contentment from ever disagreeing about which roads they mean. The predicate is handed down to the walk rather than the walk learning about cards, because the file that counts routes is a leaf and may not read the card evaluator. The happiness is paid once per town however many such carts arrive, and it goes the turn the last of them lapses. **Lives in the shared file, so lighting it changes what Expansionist deals too.** | I |
| **The Provincial Fair** | uncommon | Expansionist | built | Connected noncapital cities with a Market gain +2 food. Their worked plantations, camps and pastures gain +1 gold. | +2 food in every city joined to your capital by road but your capital with a Market · +1 gold on every hex with a Plantation or Camp or Pasture, in every city joined to your capital by road but your capital with a Market | II |
| **The Tithe** | rare | Devotion | built | Cities with a Temple gain gold equal to 25% of their base faith. Gold purchases of religious buildings there cost 30% less. | 25% of the faith in every city with a Temple is gained again as gold · faith buildings cost −30% to buy, in every city with a Temple | II |
| **The Merchant Navigators** | common | Scientific | built | Ships gain +1 movement. Routes from a city with a Harbour and a Library gain +3 science. | ships: +1 movement · +3 science on every trade route sent from every city with a Harbour with a Library | II |
| **Letters of Marque** | rare | Dominion | built | Naval combat kills grant 40 gold. Cities with a Harbour purchase naval combat units for 25% less gold, but produce those units 20% more slowly. | A kill made by one of your ships grants +40 gold · ships cost 25% less to buy in a town with a Harbour · -20% production toward ships in such a town. Nothing new was needed. This row is shared with Dominion, so lighting it changes what that deck deals too. | III |
| **The Exchange of Discoveries** | uncommon | Scientific | built | +1 science on mines and quarries on a resource. Additional +1 if the city has a market. | +1 science on every hex with a Mine or Quarry carrying a resource · the same again on those hexes in a town with a Market. Nothing new was needed. The shared file carried the card's *old* text (a count of the courts a town's caravans reach) and now carries this sheet's; the row is shared with Scientific, so both the text and the lighting change what that deck deals. | I |
| **The Cosmopolitan Court** | rare | Magisterial | built | Cities with a culture building gain +1 renown per outgoing foreign route, at most +3 per city. Great-person improvements worked by such cities gain +2 gold. | +1 renown a turn for every trade route to another empire leaving a city that holds at least one culture building, at most three per city · +2 gold on every hex carrying a great person's work in such a city. The old note was half right. The count of routes leaving a town arrived with The League of Cities and the other two. Renown counted per town did **not** already have its ceiling: a renown trickle counts the whole realm and its ceiling caps that one total, which would have let a single busy port eat the card's whole allowance. So a counted trickle may now be asked town by town, where the divisor, the ceiling and the class of town all apply once per town. The alternative — three copies of the row at three thresholds — adds up to the same figure while printing three near-identical sentences at the player, which is the near-fit this deck's house rule refuses. The coin wants a citizen standing on the work, as every hex line does. Lives in the shared file, so lighting it changes what Magisterial deals too. | III |

## Synergies with other decks

Each pair below follows the matching entry in `docs/decks/deck-design.md` ("What pairs of decks should enable"). A **hook** is something one deck's cards create that the other deck's cards read. This sheet creates its hooks whether or not the partner is seated.

### Commerce and Dominion: merchants and their guards
- **Commerce gives Dominion** purchases. Gold buys the buildings an army has no production to spare for, and buys units in an emergency.
- **Commerce gets back** protected trade routes, plunder turned into gold, and reparations from defeated empires.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** a gold reserve (The Money Lenders, The Strongroom), trade routes that need guarding (The Convoy, Entrenched Interests), and units bought with gold (The Chartered Arsenal, The Charter Fleet).
- **Hooks this sheet reads:** gold from plunder and kills fills the treasury that The Money Lenders and The Treasury Guard read.
- **Shared improvements:** mines on strategic resources. Commerce takes gold and science from them (The Mineral Trade, Strategic Reserves, Strategic Exports, Ore Caravans); Dominion builds its army on them.
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** Bought Swords, The Convoy, Professional Retainers, The Capital Arsenal, The Chartered Arsenal, The Charter Fleet, Foreign Procurement, The Paid Army, Entrenched Interests, The Treasury Guard (gold-financed strength), The Condottieri (mercenary contracts), The Company Army (a charter for a unit bought only with gold), and the shared The Escorted Roads and Letters of Marque.
- **Not carded here:** tribute (a weaker neighbour pays gold each turn instead of fighting) is closer to Dominion's mechanic and is left for Dominion's sheet; tribute already exists as a deal term. Privateers are left to Letters of Marque for now.

### Commerce and Expansionist: the land and the market
- **Commerce gives Expansionist** purchases: gold buys tiles, workers and settlers, so the empire grows faster than food alone allows.
- **Commerce gets back** goods to sell (claimed land opens resources) and surplus food to carry on trade routes.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** gold, and trade routes that carry food (Provisioning Contracts, The Home Market, the shared The Grain Exchange and Market Gardens).
- **Hooks this sheet reads:** opened resources (Salt Tithes, Luxury Caravans, Ore Caravans, Royal Assays, The Staple Right) and worked mines (Mining Districts).
- **Shared improvements:** mines and quarries. Expansionist works them for production; Commerce sells what they produce.
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** Land Speculation, Founding Capital, Purchased Prosperity, The Market Writ, Frontier Investment, Provisioning Contracts, The Home Market (market towns where several trade routes meet), The Caravanserai Network, The Waystations (tiles a trade route passes through grow richer), and the shared Market Gardens, The Grain Exchange (the grain supply) and The Provincial Fair.
- **Not carded here:** canals (a worked waterway that lets a trade route and food cross land) would be a new improvement, which is a larger decision than a card; left for the user.

### Commerce and Devotion: pilgrims and markets
- **Commerce gives Devotion** trade routes that carry religion, so faith spreads along them.
- **Commerce gets back** pilgrims: holy sites as destinations, and faith paid on trade routes.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** trade routes, and buildings bought with gold (the record The Endowment and The Waqf read).
- **Hooks this sheet reads:** holy sites (Pilgrim Markets) and cities following your religion (The Silk Road Monks).
- **Shared improvements:** plantations. Commerce takes gold and food from them (Coastal Estates, The Guild Halls); Devotion takes faith.
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** The Merchant Shrines, The Waqf (endowments), The Silk Road Monks (merchant missionaries), and the shared Pilgrim Markets (pilgrim roads) and The Tithe.
- **Gap:** neither deck covers the other's production. The pair buys with gold and with faith and builds almost nothing; the spec names it as the first pair to check in playtesting.

### Commerce and Scientific: the patrons
- **Commerce gives Scientific** gold that buys libraries and universities, and foreign trade routes that pay science.
- **Commerce gets back** technologies that open trade earlier: more trade routes, earlier ships, earlier trade buildings.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** gold and foreign trade routes, and buildings bought with gold (The Endowment pays science on each).
- **Hooks this sheet reads:** any trade unlock that arrives early is used at once by the route-capacity and range cards (The Harbour Chain, Venture Routes).
- **Shared improvements:** mines, quarries and plantations. Commerce pays gold on them; Scientific pays science (the shared The Exchange of Discoveries already does).
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** Commercial Education, Strategic Exports, The Scholars' Roads, The Endowment, The Printing Presses (gold buys science), A School of Navigation (exploration that pays science), The Harbour Copyists (books from the ships), and the shared Merchant Scholars, The Merchant Navigators and The Exchange of Discoveries.
- **Exploration:** the spec gives exploration to Commerce and asks that it be light on Scientific's sheet. Finders' Fees, The Map Sellers, The Pathfinders' Company and A Voyage of Discovery are this deck's exploration cards.

### Commerce and Magisterial: the art market
- **Commerce gives Magisterial** gold that buys rerolls and drafts, and great merchants and customs houses for its any-family cards.
- **Commerce gets back** culture turned into gold, and boons that save purchases.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** gold, a gold price on a redraw (The Brokers' Redraw) and on a great-person draft (Merchant Princes), and customs houses (The Customs Houses, The Customs Service).
- **Hooks this sheet reads:** landmarks (The Art Market, the shared The Cosmopolitan Court) and the count of decks seated in your government (the shared Travelling Players, as revised on this sheet).
- **Shared improvements:** customs houses, and landmarks on trade routes.
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** The Brokers' Redraw, Merchant Princes, A Court of Merchants, The Customs Houses, The Customs Service, The Art Market (great works on trade routes), A Guild Commission (guild commissions), The Medici Bank (patronage), and the shared Travelling Players and The Cosmopolitan Court.

## Proposed cuts
